newsitem.title: USA: Intl bank group urges change in capital standards.
newsitem.headline: Intl bank group urges change in capital standards.

text.p: A banking group Wednesday urged global supervisors to allow banks to rely entirely on sophisticated risk calculation models in computing capital charges for special parts of their portfolios.

The Institute of International Finance, Inc. argued in a report that capital requirements for "specific risks" -- individual positions in a portfolio that move more or less than the general market -- should be set according to models created by the banks themselves.
The report by the group, which includes all major international banks, was made public one day after the Basle Committee on Banking Supervision rejected its recommendations for now.

"The committee is encouraged by the progress made to date," it said in a statement issued Tuesday. But the committee said it will make changes in its requirements only "if and when the industry can provide convincing evidence that specific risk is being adequately modeled."
At a news conference, John Haseltine, deputy managing director of the IIF, characterized the Basle Committee's position this way:

"They said, 'We want to see numbers and we (the banks) replied that the numbers are confidential.'" As an alternative to providing proprietary information, the IIF suggested that the Basle Committee permit banks to model specific risks so long as the models meet certain standards.

For now, banks have two choices in setting capital standards for specific risks. They may use a standard model, which the IIF considers a crude measure that forces capital standards often higher than necessary. Or they may use their own models, but must set capital standards at least half of what they would be according to the standard model.

Barbara Matthews, banking adviser and regulatory counsel for the IIF, said that making calculations both ways is an expensive proposition that raises costs. Ultimately, she said, such costs are passed on to customers.

The action by the Basle Committee Tuesday only touched in a minor way on the question of capital charges for specific risks. Its major action was to continue to require that banks use a multiplier of three when calculating general capital risks.

Haseltine said the Basle Committee's action on general capital risks was expected but it was the industry's hope the requirement would eventually be lowered. He added that the banking community had no precise agreement on what the multiplier should be.

"We have not got any concensus among our banks as to what the ideal level is," he said. "We feel that the level may vary depending on a bank's proved efficiency in determining what the capital level needs to be to cover any tracing losses."
